title: Potentials, Risks, and Consequences of Artificial Intelligence in the Doctor-Patient Relationship
summary:
Lay medical participants are recruited and asked to first read a case description with ambiguous symptoms (upper abdominal pain and nausea after eating) and to put themselves in that situation.
Participants are then randomly assigned to one of eight groups (with equal probability of 1/8 for each group). Participants in groups 1-6 receive two diagnoses - one from an Artificial Intelligence (AI) and one from a human physician. Both information sources are simulated, i.e., no real AI and no real physician are actually used. Both diagnoses can take one of two values: low severity (heartburn/gallstone) or high severity (stomach ulcer/gallbladder inflammation). In groups 1-4 the diagnoses are conflicting. In groups 5-6 the AI and physician agree in their diagnosis. In groups 7-8, participants do not receive an AI diagnosis, but only a physician's diagnosis. After the physician diagnosis, participants are asked how much they trust the human doctor's diagnosis (primary endpoint) and whether they would like to seek a second opinion. Finally, the secondary endpoints (see below) are collected.
conditions: Medical laypeople without specified pre-existing conditions

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
None
Exclusion criteria:
We will generally include and analyse all datasets that provide responses to the primary outcome.
We will exclude all participants who completed the survey in fewer than 2 minutes indicating a lack of seriousness reading the instructions and responding to the questions. If data provide evidence for differential exclusion (i.e., if fast respondents are disproportionately found in the intervention groups), we will
perform sensitivity analyses to see the impact of fast respondents on the results.
We will also exclude all participants who answer "no" to the statement "I have answered the questions conscientiously so that they can be used for the
analyses" asked at the end of the survey
